- If sentiment is consistently low or neutral (0.00–0.20) and forecast shows strong upward trend, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If recent history shows sharp spikes followed by rapid decline, model tends to overshoot — cap forecast peak at 1–2% below true peak.  
- When sentiment is positive (0.20–0.33) and price is trending up, model often overcorrects — adjust forecast downward slightly to reflect mean reversion.  
- If forecast is flat or slowly rising while true outcome shows strong volatility, reduce forecast smoothness — allow for 1–2% deviation in early days of forecast horizon.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >5% from forecast mean in first 5–7 days, adjust model to reflect recent volatility — don’t assume trend continues unchanged.  
- If sentiment history shows no clear direction (all 0.00), forecast should not be overly optimistic — use historical mean or 10-day moving average as baseline.  
- When true outcome shows strong downward correction after a spike, model often fails to recognize it — reduce forecast slope by 10–15% in subsequent days.
